text:
Chapter Two


Nearly two weeks had gone by, and nothing could drive the kiss from Maggie’s mind. Nothing. Not all the work she needed to do to prepare her students for their final exams. Not the beautiful, warm spring weather. Nothing.


After the festival, she had returned to her apartment, a sleepy Dahlia in tow, just as the birdsong became insistent and the sky brightened to an offensive shade of pink. They had drawn the curtains tight against the onslaught of morning; drank tall, necessary glasses of water; and crashed, Maggie in her bed and Dahlia on the couch. It should have been easy for her to fall asleep, but instead Maggie tossed and turned, thinking only of the way her body had come alive under a stranger’s touch. When they had risen hours later—bleary-eyed, flowers still in their hair, and a hint of bonfire on their skin—Maggie had fessed up and told Dahlia everything.


When she thought of the kiss now, its memory felt well worn, like she had smoothed the edges by thinking of it too often. She couldn’t hold on to any details about the man, no matter how hard she tried. Not the way his hair looked in the firelight or the clothes he’d been wearing or the way he smelled. Instead, she felt branded by his touch, by his breathy whisper against the skin below her ear, by the way his body was like an answer to a question she didn’t know she’d been asking. She remembered nothing much about him, but his echo was all over her.


Unfortunately, nothing had driven the kiss from Dahlia’s mind either. Her friend had spent every spare moment over the past weeks interrogating her, combing her vague memories with an exacting precision for any hint of the man’s identity. The first thing Dahlia said to Maggie as she walked up to join her for lunch by the giant, ancient hawthorn tree that gave their college its name was, “What if we did a scrying spell?”


Maggie took a bite of her sandwich, wondering if it was worth it to try to ignore this question, but she knew Dahlia would only continue the conversation without her.


“And put what, exactly, into the calculation?” Scrying runes worked if you knew what you were looking for. The precise calculations necessary to complete the rune required specific details about the missing person or object. They knew nothing that would be useful.


“Have you remembered anything new?” Dahlia asked as she shook her container of salad.


“I remember looking up at him as we danced, so he was taller than me,” she recited, though Dahlia had already heard it a dozen times. “And I remember what he told me. That’s it.”


Dahlia stabbed her fork into a cherry tomato with more force than was strictly necessary. “I still can’t believe you found Galloway’s tallest eligible bachelor and you didn’t let him take off his mask.”


There had been many moments since she left the beach when Maggie had wondered at her own decision, regretted it even. The mask taunted her from its new home, hanging from her car’s rearview mirror, its hawthorn petals drying to cellophane. But she knew, without a doubt, that she would still make the same choice if he were in front of her now. She would rather dream about what might have been, maddening as it was, than let someone in.



—


In her Introduction to Phonology course a few hours later, Maggie threw open the windows to catch an errant breeze as she watched her first-year students complete their quiz on the interdimensional phonetic alphabet. However they did on this quiz would help her shape her review lessons before the final exam in a few weeks, which made her almost as nervous as they were. Would she spend the next few weeks frantically reviewing the basics, or could they dive deeper into some interesting topics that might entice some of the students to keep studying linguistics? She’d know soon enough.


Her students were restless—noses scrunched, tapping pencil erasers and fanning themselves with spare pieces of paper. Peals of laughter drifted up to the classroom from outside, where students who were already free of their classes had shed sweaters for T-shirts and sundresses to enjoy the warm weather.


“Five more minutes,” Maggie said as she weaved through the desks. One student sighed in relief or frustration, Maggie wasn’t sure which, and pencils began scratching faster across paper.


The first sign that something was very wrong came when the flickering faefire lamps hanging from the ceiling began to swing on their dainty chains. Maggie looked up quizzically. She was watching the ornate pendants and the dust shaken free from their shades when a cacophonous crash shook the floor above them. Confusion more than fear rippled through the classroom as her students followed her gaze as if they would be able to see through the ceiling to whatever caused the ruckus.


At first, Maggie thought one of the transmutation lectures had gotten particularly unruly. It wouldn’t be the first time that one of Jim’s demonstrations turning a cockroach into a mouse led to knocked-over chairs and frightened second years, but then there was another crash.


Somewhere upstairs, glass shattered. The floor shook again. There was shouting and a high-pitched scream. Maggie’s heart raced, even as she reminded her students to remain calm. But none of them could deny the unmistakable odor of magic gone wrong—sulfur and the burnt tinge of ether—that was now seeping into her classroom from above.


“I think it’s time to evacuate.” The easy tone of Maggie’s voice belied her worry. Her students glanced at one another nervously, like fawns, but obeyed the careful instructions she recited, filing slowly out of the classroom toward the nearest stairwell. In the hall, the smell was overwhelming, and they tucked their noses into their collars and sputtered coughs.


Ilex Hall was an old manor house that had been converted into classrooms eighty-odd years before, when the property became Hawthorn College. Square-shaped with a courtyard in the middle, there were rounded turrets with sprawling spiral staircases in each corner. Maggie directed her students to the northern stairwell while she cataloged the possibilities of what had gone wrong.


A fire in one of the alchemy labs on the third floor, filled with countless chemicals and equipment, would be a nightmare. It could, she supposed, be a ghoul. They weren’t unheard of this close to the Wilds and were sometimes drawn to campus by their insatiable hunger, though how it would have gotten all the way to the third floor without anyone noticing, she had no idea. She was thinking through their evacuation route and the dangers they might encounter when Beth, the student in the front of the line, screeched, “What the fuck is that?”


Maggie pushed her way forward. The heavy antique door that led to the stairwell oozed a lavender-tinged sludge, and Maggie blanched. Damn. In all the possibilities she had sorted through, this was not one of them.


“That is pall slime,” she said, breathless. “Stay behind me.” The mouths of her students dropped in shock, new alarm widening their eyes as they shuffled behind her. Beth wiped her hands aggressively on her jeans.


Maggie’s students knew well enough the hazards of a pall, even if they’d never seen one before. Palls were the dangerous by-products of powerful alchemical reactions gone wrong. The energy required for spellmaking had to come from somewhere. Small, everyday spells took only a little bit, like plucking a piece of lint off a sweater. Big spells took so much more, and, when things went wrong, they could cause a snag, a rip in the fabric that separates this world from the next. That was a pall.


A misplaced line in a rune, a mispronounced incantation, the incorrect ratio of ingredients in a decoction—if the magic was strong enough, if the power needed to initiate the transformation great enough, even a small slipup could cause a pall. Palls caused untold havoc, including producing otherworldly debris like the strange slime.


“I thought only big spells could produce a pall. Why is there one here?” one of her students asked.


“That’s a great question,” Maggie muttered as she took out the spare bit of chalk she kept in her pocket. They all knew the rules. Class 3 spells are strictly prohibited on Hawthorn College’s campus without the proper protocols. Most spells did not have enough power behind them to produce a pall, and only the most experienced alchemists should even attempt the ones that did. She hadn’t done magic that powerful without some form of magical training wheels until a full year into grad school. She couldn’t imagine which of her colleagues had let such a thing happen.


“Anyone have the time?” she called over her shoulder, and a student provided it down to the second. Maggie did a quick calculation in her head and began to draw a rune on the door.


“In an emergency,” she explained, taking advantage of the situation to get in a little instruction, “we go for the simplest rune with the highest impact.” Her hands shook—with adrenaline, with fear—but she managed straight-enough lines. “Until we contain this pall, even mistakes on simple spells will feed it. The last thing we want to do right now is make this thing worse.”


When the rune was complete, she placed her palm on the chalk lines and said the Diadhan incantation to activate it—a simple phrase that invoked a temporary but impermeable seal. Her chalk lines glowed bright, followed by a dim shimmer that slid around the gap between the frame and the door. It sealed with a pop, cutting off the source of the lavender sludge.


“We’re not going to panic,” she told herself as much as her students as she watched the door to make sure her barrier spell held. “Brief exposure to a pall won’t cause lasting damage, and this rune should keep it contained, but we do need to find another way out of the building.” The unsaid hung in the air among them—more than a brief exposure was dangerous. In the short term, it could cause a host of physical effects like nausea, vomiting, and fatigue. In the long term…well, Maggie wasn’t even going to think about that right now. Hopefully the other stairwell was clear.


When she was confident no more slime was oozing through the cracks in the door, Maggie herded her students through the hallway toward the other stairs. It was absolute chaos. Students darted around, shouting at one another and swarming the stairwells. Maggie spotted Dahlia, shepherding her own students through the mayhem.


“Dahlia!” she shouted over the din. “It’s a pall.” Even through the crowd, Maggie saw Dahlia mutter a curse under her breath. “Is the south stair clear?” Dahlia pushed her way through the gathered students, taking only a moment before she was back, waving everyone on.


When Maggie finally reached Dahlia, the other professor was still muttering under her breath. “Do those dingbats in Alchemy know the rest of this building is full of people?” Maggie shrugged as she held the door open, counting her students as they evacuated the hall one by one.


“It filled the northern stairwell,” Maggie told Dahlia, still not quite believing it herself. Though they were dangerous, most palls could be quickly contained and dissipated, becoming more of a nuisance than a real threat. They were cleared up before they caused significant damage, or they were sealed into a small space. Maggie understood that, theoretically, a pall could fill an entire building, but she’d never seen it. Never even heard of it.


Another crash startled Maggie, Dahlia, and the students streaming past them, who all ducked in unison as if the floor above them was about to cave in. Maggie braced herself, but then the door on the landing above sprang open, and coughing, sputtering students spilled out. Pall slime coated their clothing, iridescent and smelling strongly of sulfur, and their hair was dotted with heavy dust. Apart from the greenish, nauseated looks on their faces, they were in one piece. Maggie ushered them forward to join the throng of students exiting the building.


When she was satisfied that all the students from the second floor were on their way out of Ilex Hall to safety on the lawn, hopefully following the evacuation protocol they had gone over on the first day of class, Maggie turned to Dahlia. “I’m going up to make sure everyone is out. Can you keep my students with yours at the meeting point?”


They parted ways, with Dahlia impatiently running behind the last student and Maggie going against every instinct in her body to run up toward the pall. Adrenaline pushed her up the stairs. When she reached the third-floor landing, she eased a stitch in her side with one hand and took out her chalk with the other.


As she pressed her chalk into the old wood grain of the door to draw the first line of the rune, it opened suddenly and knocked her back. Her stomach dropped as she lost her balance, tilting toward the stairs behind her. She waved her arms wildly, trying to find anything to hold on to, trying to regain her balance, but then a strong hand gripped her forearm and pulled her upright while slamming the door shut again.


“We need to evacuate the building now,” the man who grabbed her snarled as Maggie caught her breath, her hands on her knees as she thanked the gods below for the solid ground beneath her feet.


“What do you think we’ve been doing?” she snapped. Fortunately, she had not lost her chalk in her near fall, so she returned to the door and began drawing the rune again. The man pulled a handkerchief from his pocket and wiped away her work. “Hey!”


“We need something stronger than this,” he huffed.


“Not if there are still students or staff in here!” Anything stronger would lock people inside the hallway with the pall, unable to get around the powerful magic he was suggesting they use to stop it from spreading.


He whipped around to face Maggie. In the frenzy, she hadn’t gotten a good look at him after he grabbed her, and she hadn’t stopped to consider whom she might be yelling at.


Arthur Taliesin. The Arthur Taliesin. Lead alchemist and director of the labs on the third floor. Son of the late internationally renowned alchemist Rowena Taliesin and famous in his own right. They stood shoulder to shoulder in front of the door and Maggie’s ruined rune. She nearly tipped back again trying to get a good look at him.


Maggie was not a small woman, but Taliesin towered over her. He looked down his nose at her, and his features sorted themselves into an impressive scowl. His skin was unusually pale, surely because of his exposure to the pall, contrasting starkly against dark brown, nearly black hair that had fallen from its styling into his eyes. His wire-framed glasses were smudged with dusty fingerprints, and his sweater was dotted with pall slime. Somehow, none of it made him any less handsome, a fact that annoyed Maggie greatly.


She had been a little starstruck when Taliesin joined the faculty in the fall, they all had been, but it had faded quickly. Taliesin was aloof and rude on a good day, and she’d been avoiding him since a particularly contentious budget meeting in November when she’d learned exactly the kind of person he was.


“My lab is the only one with a three p.m. session, and I sure as hell didn’t leave any of my students in there,” he said angrily, a bite of indignation in his voice. Maggie’s expression of surprise melted into a scowl to rival Taliesin’s. If Arthur Taliesin’s Materials Alchemy class was the only one in session, that must mean the pall formed in his lab. She had thought of Taliesin as many things—rude, inconsiderate, pompous—but she’d never thought of him as incompetent or reckless. “Now get out of here before the pall slips through this door and makes the rest of this building uninhabitable.”


As if on cue, the force of the growing pall pressed against the door and it creaked on its hinges. Slime oozed through the cracks, and Maggie gagged on the smell. Instead of listening to Taliesin, she threw her weight against the door. He huffed in disapproval and patted his pockets, looking for his own piece of chalk. “Godsdamn it,” he spat when he came up empty. Maggie held out her chalk with a self-satisfied smirk that Taliesin did not return.


He took it from her palm and, above her head, drew the more complicated symbol, his movements elegant and his rune lines more confident than her own. The door creaked again, and Taliesin added his weight to hers, their shoulders pressing together as they leaned into the door and Taliesin spoke the incantation aloud. Maggie noted that his pronunciation of the Diadhan words left something to be desired and she would have, perhaps, used a slightly different translation for the word seal, but it didn’t matter. The rune activated, and pall slime stopped oozing through the cracks. Maggie and Taliesin sagged against the door, spent.


Some of the slime dripped down onto Maggie’s arm, and she wiped it away as best she could with a grimace. Taliesin pushed off the door, pocketed her chalk, and started toward the stairs without so much as a thank-you for her help. “You know,” she muttered as she followed behind him, “you could have asked the Diadhan scholar to say the incantation.” If Taliesin heard her, he didn’t acknowledge it. Instead, he patted the pocket where he’d placed her chalk just moments before.


There was another drawn-out creak from the door hinges, and both professors looked upward, but his spell held. “We should seal the other doors,” she said, her annoyance momentarily forgotten.


“No.” Well, he certainly heard that. “I will seal the other doors. You need to get out of here.” He didn’t wait for her response and jogged down the rest of the stairs, but Maggie was close on his heels. He stopped on the second-floor landing, his hand on the doorknob to the hall. “Don’t follow me, Maggie.”


Maggie stopped. She didn’t know Arthur Taliesin knew her name at all, and it startled her enough that she stared after him as he disappeared into the second-floor hall. She nearly followed him, resigning herself to putting up with his scowl and disdain, when she decided that he was right.


Something had happened in his lab that had exposed them all to this giant, disastrous pall. He was the one responsible, and he certainly didn’t seem to want her help. He could clean up his own mess. He seemed perfectly capable. Besides, she needed to check on her students.


They were gathered on the sweeping lawn in front of the building, huddled together with Dahlia’s students beneath the hawthorn where Maggie and Dahlia had eaten lunch just a few hours earlier. “I counted forty-two. Eighteen of them are mine,” Dahlia said. “It’s like herding cats trying to keep them all together.”


“That’s all of them. There are twenty-four in my intro course.” Maggie leaned against the tree beside Dahlia, finally giving her heart a chance to slow down. When it no longer felt like it was going to beat out of her chest, she said, “You’ll never guess who came out of that pall.”


“I haven’t got a clue. Who would be dumb enough to let their students mess with magic dangerous enough to produce a pall?”


“Arthur Taliesin.” Maggie kept her voice low so none of the students milling around might grow interested in their conversation. Dahlia’s mouth dropped in shock.


“No way.” As if in confirmation, the doors to Ilex Hall crashed open and Taliesin spilled out onto the steps. He was barely upright, but one of his slime-covered students, fortified by the sunshine and warm air, went over to help him down the stairs. Taliesin waved him off, and Maggie didn’t even try to contain her eye roll. Couldn’t the guy take help when it was offered?


Even at this distance, Taliesin looked rough. Maggie had severely underestimated how much of the pall he’d breathed in. His skin had gone from pale to slightly green, and he looked like he was about to lose his lunch at any moment. These were classic symptoms of pall exposure, along with the fatigue clearly plaguing him.


Starting with Taliesin’s own students, a smattering of applause started up and swelled through the crowd. Maggie rolled her eyes again and Dahlia bristled. “Man saves the day from self-inflicted catastrophe,” Maggie muttered.


“Alert the media,” Dahlia finished, and Maggie flashed her friend a wicked grin.


Taliesin lifted a hand slowly in appreciation of the applause and finally took the assistance of another alchemy professor, who held him up as they limped toward the infirmary.


“It’s going to take time to clear out that pall,” Dahlia complained. “Everything is going to stink like ether and death.”


“At least your apartment is on the other side of town,” Maggie whined. “This thing is going to attract every wraith, ghoul, and banshee for miles. I’m never sleeping again.”


“I told you being able to walk to work was overrated.” Dahlia had, in fact, mentioned something of the sort. Maggie leaned her head against the hawthorn tree, suddenly exhausted now that the imminent danger had passed. Hopefully the pall would be nothing but a nuisance now. Fantasmia—especially the ghouls, banshees, and wraiths that would be drawn to the otherworldly magic—would be more frequent, but there were protections against them. Having the third floor cut off from the rest of the building during the rush to the end of the semester would be the worst of it. A dissipation spell would have to be crafted, but it shouldn’t take more than a few days.


Her students had already scattered, their panic forgotten in the sunshine. A game of Frisbee had picked up where it left off, and someone had started blasting music. The sound had a tinny, far-off quality that told Maggie the student was using some kind of rune to amplify it but had misjudged the calculations. Whatever gets them to practice.


Maggie stared up at the windows of the third floor of Ilex Hall. The pall was visible, giving the glass a deep purple tint. Inside, the swirling unease of gas and dust and slime that made up the pall passed by the windows, illuminated by the faefire lights that flashed with the surge of magic. The pall looked alive as it undulated through classrooms, offices, and labs. When a particularly bright cloud moved by one window, she could just make out a rune on the glass, drawn in the same careful strokes she had seen in the hallway when Taliesin had stolen her chalk. Each window, she now saw, held the same rune, drawn in the same careful hand. She turned, just in time, to see Taliesin hobble into the building that housed the infirmary.

facts.fact: 吻后两周：细节全忘、触感留存（his echo was all over her）。
facts.anchor: his echo was all over her

facts.fact: Dahlia 提议 scrying spell；Maggie 反驳需要目标具体信息而她们一无所知。
facts.anchor: Scrying runes worked if you knew what you were looking for

facts.fact: 面具挂后视镜嘲弄她；她确认重来一次仍会拒绝——宁愿梦着也不放人进来。
facts.anchor: She would rather dream about what might have been

facts.fact: 课上 faefire 灯晃、楼上巨响，硫磺混乙醚气味渗入——Ilex Hall 出事。
facts.anchor: the unmistakable odor of magic gone wrong

facts.fact: 楼梯门渗淡紫淤泥：她认出 pall slime，画符文+Diadhan 咒封门，带学生走南梯。
三楼开门者是 Arthur Taliesin（首席炼金术师、Rowena 之子）；他抹她的符文、抢粉笔画更强封印。
他喊 Don't follow me, Maggie——她惊觉他叫得出她的名字；草坪点数 42 名学生。
三楼下午三点唯一有课的是他的 Materials Alchemy——pall 出自他的实验室；他被搀去医务室。
facts.anchor: Materials Alchemy class was the only one in session
